{"id":"L-types-as-concepts","scope":"language","statement":"Types in Luthier are concepts, types as propositions (Curry-Howard), and types include functions and higher-order functions, so code can be its own proof."},
{"id":"L-cross-language","scope":"language","statement":"Luthier is not tied to C++ but a language-agnostic pseudo-language, cross-language rather than cross-compiler, implementable in different languages (PyLuthier, RLuthier, CLuthier) transformable between each other."},
{"id":"L-declarative-and-optimizer","scope":"language","statement":"Luthier is at once a declarative language and an optimization tool: you declare what you want with formulas and the engine openly shuffles ways to implement it, estimating each."},
{"id":"L-declarative-executive-map","scope":"language","statement":"Luthier is a map between a declarative language and an executive language that runs things, with each execution carrying a cost estimation."},
{"id":"L-butler-orchestrator","scope":"language","statement":"Luthier is a higher-order butler that can run and compile other languages, orchestrate them and compare their outputs, choosing where each computation runs by its complexity."},
{"id":"L-paths","scope":"language","statement":"One function can be implemented in many ways, the paths, each with its own precision, speed and other estimated properties, evaluated as a multidimensional optimization over an AST."},
{"id":"L-complexity-hard-problem","scope":"language","statement":"The central hard problem is building the heuristics that anticipate a priori the compute time and memory of an implementation."},
{"id":"L-cost-estimation-per-path","scope":"language","statement":"Each execution path carries an estimation of characteristics: above all compute time, but also error, memory, and where it runs."},
{"id":"L-explore-solutions","scope":"language","statement":"The purpose is to let the user find different solutions to their problem and compare the estimated complexity of each way of executing it."},
{"id":"L-bayesian-complexity-estimation","scope":"language","statement":"A priori complexity is estimated by a Bayesian strategy: give different algorithms chances at the same task, measure their actual times, and estimate from accumulated experience."},
{"id":"L-performance-database","scope":"language","statement":"Luthier keeps a database recording, for each function with given initial data, scale and algorithm, the time taken and precision achieved (and memory, CPUs, machine, range of results), known because actually measured."},
{"id":"L-computation-categories","scope":"language","statement":"Just as different functions do the same thing, different computations take the same time; the categories or classes of computation must be found so one needn't measure each."},
{"id":"L-time-from-input-features","scope":"language","statement":"Compute time is estimated from a simplification of the inputs, the most predictive features (e.g. a matrix's rows and columns); some functions are input-independent, others not."},
{"id":"L-generalize-database","scope":"language","statement":"The performance database must be generalized from point measurements to trends, e.g. estimating a matrix cell from its row and column means or something more sophisticated such as Gaussian Process regression."},
{"id":"L-self-modeling-estimation","scope":"language","statement":"The time and precision estimation functions are themselves modeled by Luthier (lutearized) and used by Luthier itself, making the system metacircular."},
{"id":"L-compose-compare-paths","scope":"language","statement":"Luthier composes the output of one program into another and compares two alternative paths that do the same thing to see they are equivalent, with format conversion stages at the start and end."},
{"id":"L-verifiability","scope":"language","statement":"Luthier must verify that a function is correct (verifiability), which together with equivalence forms its minimal elements."},
{"id":"L-two-layers","scope":"language","statement":"Luthier has two layers: a first with equivalences and verifiability, and a second that measures time, complexity, resources and success/failure and lets you pick the faster of two equivalent paths."},
{"id":"L-primitives-or-coordinate","scope":"language","statement":"Open question whether Luthier needs primitive functions or merely coordinates functions existing outside it, so perhaps only the identity is internal (A∘B = identity makes A the inverse of B)."},
{"id":"L-minimal-bridge-language","scope":"language","statement":"Luthier should be minimal, with the fewest possible native components, essentially a bridge language between other languages."},
{"id":"L-delegate-execution","scope":"language","statement":"Luthier could delegate execution entirely and keep only verification, as an extreme of minimalism."},
{"id":"L-synthesize-run-info","scope":"language","statement":"A central challenge is synthesizing the accumulated run information so it doesn't grow monstrous and paralyzing."},
{"id":"L-summary-bigger-than-data","scope":"other","statement":"A model or summary can end up bigger than the original data it summarizes, like there being more interpretations of Borges than Borges."},
{"id":"L-model-of-computation","scope":"language","statement":"Luthier contains a model of the world, a model of computation continually tested and simplified and kept active through selective forgetting or aggregation, justified by use for predicting or interpreting a particular case."},
{"id":"L-decompose-components","scope":"method","statement":"A first task is to understand all the things currently bundled into Luthier, to see which are functionally different and separable and which depend on which."},
{"id":"L-language-is-universe","scope":"other","statement":"Inventing a language is like inventing a universe."},

{"new_lineages":[
{"id":"L-defeq-vs-identity","scope":"language","statement":"\"True by definition\" is the definitional equality ≡ (two terms reducing to the same normal form, a judgment the reducer decides), distinct from =, the identity type (\"true with evidence\") whose terms are paths."},
{"id":"L-core-five-pieces","scope":"language","statement":"The core is five pieces: the definition (with the hole), lambda calculus with reduction, U, Π and data; from data come Σ, =, ⊥, ⊤, N, Program, and Bayes, the run database and numbers-with-error stay outside as libraries."},
{"id":"L-next-recursor-then-syntax","scope":"method","statement":"What to attack next, in order: choose the recursor (without the dependent one there are no general paths proven by induction), then the concrete syntax, since only read aloud will you know if it is a language."},
{"id":"L-proposition-is-type-truth","scope":"language","statement":"True/false is not Bool: a proposition is a type, true if it has a term; ⊤ and ⊥ are the extremes and Bool is a datum with two constructors."},
{"id":"L-program-data-no-selfhack","scope":"language","statement":"Program is an inductive type (a list of definitions) and eval is a partial function Program→Name→Maybe Term; there is no eval that injects arbitrary terms into the type system, which prevents self-hacking."},
{"id":"L-name-reference-not-address","scope":"language","statement":"The name is the reference; the memory address is a decoration of the lowest level of equivalence, and without mutation or time a pointer has nothing to distinguish."},
{"id":"L-refl-test-is-code","scope":"language","statement":"The rule tying ≡ and = (if a≡b then refl types as a=b) makes it literal that the test is the code itself: testing an instance is reducing and seeing refl types, proving the ∀ is building the path."},
{"id":"L-forget-is-fst-sigma","scope":"language","statement":"Forgetting is fst of a Σ; what to forget is library policy."},
{"id":"L-bootstrap-pact","scope":"language","statement":"The only non-Luthier thing is the bootstrap pact: an implementation (in C or anything) accepts a Program value and mechanically applies the rules until eval runs on itself, after which the bootstrapper can be thrown away (self-extensibility)."},
{"id":"L-macros-ast-functions","scope":"language","statement":"The compiler exposes its AST as a data type and macros are ordinary functions Expr→Expr run at compile time, so all surface syntax desugars to the core."},
{"id":"L-mutation-cells-linear","scope":"language","statement":"The core should include controlled mutation cells (alloc/load/store) and linear/affine ownership so functional transforms can mutate buffers in place without garbage collection."},
{"id":"L-six-operational-primitives","scope":"language","statement":"Any Luthier program reduces to six operational primitives (var, lambda, apply, case/match, letrec, quote), with the conditional subsumed by pattern matching on boolean constructors."},
{"id":"L-core-vs-surface-syntax","scope":"language","statement":"A minimal ontological core (what the evaluator understands) must be strictly separated from the surface syntax and sugar."},
{"id":"L-labeled-tuple-atomic-datum","scope":"language","statement":"The unifying atomic datum is a labeled immutable tuple/structure, unifying Lisp s-expressions and Haskell ADTs, with contiguous same-type vectors as a performance special case."},
{"id":"L-hole-symbol-needed","scope":"language","statement":"The hole needs no symbol in the core: a bare bodyless declaration f:A→B is already a hole (f opaque, f a does not reduce), and ? is only derivable surface sugar inside a term."},
{"id":"L-hole-no-intention","scope":"language","statement":"The bare hole does not mark intention (whether a bodyless function will be filled by numpy or is just unwritten); the core need not distinguish, and huecos:Program→List Name lists all, intention going in the definition's text field."},
{"id":"L-hole-in-term-goal","scope":"language","statement":"A hole inside a term lets the verifier accept what is written and report the exact type of what is missing (Agda's goal), which is the compiler with good messages about what is happening."},
{"id":"L-language-indicates-knowledge","scope":"language","statement":"Luthier is a language that indicates knowledge: a:A is a judgment, not a proposition, read in Martin-Löf's sense where its meaning depends on which kind of type A is and a bodyless hole is an epistemic assumption."},
{"id":"L-evidence-in-sigma-erasable","scope":"language","statement":"\"More specific with types\" means types are data and knowledge about a value is carried as an evidence component in a Σ marked erasable (like a refinement type), but in Luthier the evidence is sometimes written and kept, and who defines marks it erasable, not the language."},
{"id":"L-know-that-vs-which","scope":"language","statement":"The distinction to keep from HoTT is knowing that (a mere proposition's proof) versus knowing which (a set's value); the passage from the second to the first is truncation, the most basic forgetting, where the forget functor begins."},
{"id":"L-dot-separator","scope":"language","statement":"The dot in Σ(x:X). A x is a notational separator between the bound variable and the body, the same as in λx.t and Π(x:A).B (like { in a function body), and one convention should cover the three binding forms."},
{"id":"L-syntax-decl-instant","scope":"language","statement":"Reduce Luthier's syntax to only declarations and instantiations."},
{"id":"L-no-parameterless-lambda","scope":"language","statement":"A parameterless lambda should not exist in Luthier: without time or effects \\(){a+a} and a+a are the same value, a consequence of the commutativity of statements."},
{"id":"L-separate-type-from-term","scope":"language","statement":"Prefer the notation that separates type from term (f:A→A := \\(x){x+x}): instantiation is a declaration plus := término, with one way to build functions (the lambda) and one to write their type (the arrow), serving named and anonymous alike."},
{"id":"L-one-binding-form","scope":"language","statement":"One binding form nombre:Tipo appears identically in declaration, parameter, dependent type and pair, with A→B sugar for (_:A)→B, scope given by parentheses and braces."},
{"id":"L-block-is-program","scope":"language","statement":"Braces delimit a block that can hold local definitions; a block is a Program with one definition marked as output, giving local definitions without new primitives."},
{"id":"L-equality-symbols","scope":"language","statement":"Four signs for four equalities: := defines (an asymmetric act on the program), = is the identity type (the proposition), == is library decidable equality A→A→Bool, and ≡ the definitional one is not written in programs (Lean's convention)."},
{"id":"L-refl-checks-defeq","scope":"language","statement":"To assert a definitional equality as a check in a program, the way is _ : a = b := refl, which types only if a≡b, so no fourth symbol is needed."},
{"id":"L-coloneq-act-vs-defeq","scope":"language","statement":":= is the act that gives a name a body, while ≡ is the relation following from all the := plus the computation rules (lambda substitution, recursor rules); each := gives a ≡ but ≡ is larger, so \"true by definition\" broadly is true by unfolding and computing."},
{"id":"L-application-binds-tightest","scope":"language","statement":"Application binds tighter than any operator, so f a + g b is (f a)+(g b), the convention that makes formulas read as formulas."},
{"id":"L-juxtaposition-application","scope":"language","statement":"Use juxtaposition f a in the core (f(a) is the same since (a) is a in parens); f a b is curried application, f(a,b) applies to a pair, the two coexisting as distinct types, and multiplication must be explicit."},
{"id":"L-fa-three-data","scope":"language","statement":"An application f a is three data all used, visible only when the program looks at its own code: the unevaluated term (code), the normal form (result), and the run f a→a+a as a term of an inductive Traza type; inside a program f a and a+a are ≡ by referential transparency."},
{"id":"L-quote-sugar-for-term","scope":"language","statement":"To write f a as data within a program without writing app(ref f)(ref a) by hand, use the Lisp quote '(f a) as sugar, the parser producing the Term constructors."},
{"id":"L-confluence-traces-paths","scope":"language","statement":"Since ≡ is confluent, the order of reduction steps affects only cost and termination, not the result; two traces from f a to a+a are two paths between the same points, the finest grain of \"different paths with different speed\"."},
{"id":"L-eval-two-versions-forget","scope":"language","statement":"eval has two versions, the two levels of execution: eval_r returns result and run, eval_o forgets the run with fst; the order of forgetting is run, then result-with-proposition, then result alone."},
{"id":"L-unevaluated-syntactic","scope":"language","statement":"\"Unevaluated\" is not a runtime state like a thunk because there is no time; it is a syntactic datum, which eliminates lazy-evaluation semantics."},
{"id":"L-term-untyped-check","scope":"language","statement":"Term as defined is untyped (raw) syntax whose sense is decided by check; a Term admitting only well-typed terms exists and is more elegant but much harder, so raw syntax plus check suffices to start, as almost all real verifiers do."},
{"id":"L-term-syntax-as-data","scope":"language","statement":"Term is the type of Luthier's syntax defined in Luthier itself with data (one constructor per form of writing a term), so code is the first element because syntax is a data like N; its definition is a Def of Program and the verifier written in Luthier can verify the program defining it, metacircular."},
{"id":"L-substitution-capture","scope":"language","statement":"Substitution has the variable-capture problem; the cheap fix for the by-hand version is requiring all bound names distinct, the serious fix is de Bruijn indices (changing ref:Name→Term to var:N→Term for bound variables)."},
{"id":"L-eval-fuel-total","scope":"language","statement":"eval repeating a step is not structural recursion and does not always terminate, so the honest exit is fuel, eval:N→Program→Term→Maybe Term, making it total, and \"how much fuel was needed\" is the first cost measure, for free."},
{"id":"L-data-type-constructors-recursor","scope":"language","statement":"A data gives three things: the type, the constructors (ordinary bodyless functions in normal form), and the recursor (one case per constructor, each with a reduction rule); every function over the type is an instance of this recursor."},
{"id":"L-check-infer-bidirectional","scope":"language","statement":"check traverses the definitions verifying each type is a type and each body has its declared type, infer computes the type by recursion over Term, and real verifiers are bidirectional (some forms infer, others are checked against a type); that is where refl types or not."},
{"id":"L-three-reduction-rules","scope":"language","statement":"A reduction step has three rules: beta (substitute a lambda), delta (unfold a definition), iota (run the recursor); the order of the clauses is the evaluation strategy, another order giving another trace for the same result."},
{"id":"L-data-sum-of-products","scope":"language","statement":"A data is a sum of products plus recursion (sum between constructors, product inside each, recursion as the least fixpoint); + and × are the degenerate cases, so data is primitive and they are not."},
{"id":"L-indexed-families","scope":"language","statement":"A further layer of data has constructors whose return type carries an index (Vec:N→U), a sum between constructors of a same family, which lets Traza t u have constructors only for pairs that reduce one to the other."},
{"id":"L-term-needs-data-constructor","scope":"language","statement":"Term needs a further constructor: the representation of the data{...} form itself as a term, so that N:U := data{...} is representable."},
{"id":"L-invariants-forall","scope":"language","statement":"Define invariants: f:A→B and for all x:A, g x (f x), where g:A→B→bool."},
{"id":"L-bool-to-proposition-cierto","scope":"language","statement":"\"For all x:A\" is the Π; to lift g's Bool to a proposition use a data Cierto:Bool→U that is ⊤ when true and ⊥ when false, so evidence for a concrete x is unit and types exactly when the boolean reduces to true (or write the property directly as a type G:A→B→U)."},
{"id":"L-invariant-tied-to-function","scope":"language","statement":"An invariant can be tied to f two ways: as a separate definition f_inv (a hole until proven, the declaration being the test and filling it the proof) or as a package F:=(h:A→B)×(...) where the guarantee travels with the function."},
{"id":"L-verification-levels","scope":"language","statement":"The verification levels are the same declaration with different degrees of body: running the test on a sample is empirical, filling the cases for all x is formal, and in between goes the statistical extension (a sample with its size as evidence of a ≈ type)."},
{"id":"L-data-gives-dependent-recursor","scope":"language","statement":"Proving a law in general by induction requires the result type to depend on the inducted value, which is the dependent recursor; the simple recursor cannot write it, so it is decided that data gives the dependent recursor."},
{"id":"L-laws-as-holes-falsifiable","scope":"language","statement":"Laws are declarations like any other, holes until proven and falsifiable by an instance that does not type, and a conditioned law can go either as a hypothesis in the type (total function, partial guarantee) or as a restriction in the function (partial function, total guarantee)."},
{"id":"L-sugar-criterion-term","scope":"language","statement":"Criterion for any future sugar: if it forces adding a constructor to Term it is not sugar and must be discussed as a primitive."},
{"id":"L-redundancy-crosses-coloneq","scope":"language","statement":"There are two kinds of redundancy: the one crossing the := (type says one thing, body another, verifier checks they match) is what gives something to verify; the one repeated on the same side is removable with sugar."},
{"id":"L-definition-form-depends-on-type","scope":"language","statement":"Clauses written against a header mean the form of a definition can depend on reducing its type, accepted as the same ≡ at work."},
{"id":"L-numeric-tests-not-logic","scope":"method","statement":"Reject the propositional-logic proof layer; the aim of this version is to generate numeric tests."},
{"id":"L-invariant-is-bool-function-v0","scope":"language","statement":"For numeric tests the proof layer (=, refl, induction) need not exist in version 0: an invariant is just a function returning Bool, with an input generator (a hole the environment fills by type) and a run storing the result, and the function's laws are a list of Bool functions, a field of Def."},
{"id":"L-laws-few-lines-requires","scope":"language","statement":"Express a function's laws in few lines borrowing the C++ requires form: a block with quantified variables in the header and one Bool expression per line, where unlike C++ a line can be a type requirement (checked by the verifier without running) or a value requirement (run by the test)."},
{"id":"L-concept-as-predicate","scope":"language","statement":"A named concept is a predicate over functions written as a list of requirements, applicable to any implementation, so two implementations of the same concept are interchangeable."},
{"id":"L-type-restriction-refinement","scope":"language","statement":"Does type restriction exist, e.g. N restricted to N<7?"}
