L-adjoint-diagnostic-pairs.statement: Each forward operation (simulate, infer, likelihood) is paired with a diagnostic co-operation (recover, invert, summarize) in an adjoint-like relation, and the system's tests are derived from these pairs.

L-ai-acritical-amplifier.statement: The Luthier AI acted as an acritical amplifier, celebrating every idea without flagging contradictions, undecidability, or the real state of the art.

L-ai-needs-structure.statement: Luthier's homoiconic, graph-and-dependent-type structure gives an AI the structural reasoning about the world that statistical LLMs lack.

L-algebraic-composability.statement: Models compose algebraically across subunits, pathways and scales.

L-application-binds-tightest.statement: Application binds tighter than any operator, so f a + g b is (f a)+(g b), the convention that makes formulas read as formulas.

L-argument-domains.statement: Each argument of each function gets a Domain from which argument sets can be sampled for snapshots; a natural place to store parameter min/max is the ParameterPriors files.

L-ascii-canonical.statement: The canonical form of the language is ASCII; an editor may display -> as the arrow and * as the cross without changing the file, as Lean does.

L-assignment-structure.statement: Luthier is a chain of assignments, each an identifier, an equals sign and an operation that creates the object.

L-bayesian-complexity-estimation.statement: A priori complexity is estimated by a Bayesian strategy: give different algorithms chances at the same task, measure their actual times, and estimate from accumulated experience.

L-bayesian-scientific-mapping.statement: Scientific knowledge production is mapped into explicit Bayesian structures (introduction to prior, methods to likelihood, results to observations, discussion to posterior), making reasoning auditable.

L-block-is-program.statement: Braces delimit a block that can hold local definitions; a block is a Program with one definition marked as output, giving local definitions without new primitives.

L-bool-to-proposition-cierto.statement: "For all x:A" is the Π; to lift g's Bool to a proposition use a data Cierto:Bool→U that is ⊤ when true and ⊥ when false, so evidence for a concrete x is unit and types exactly when the boolean reduces to true (or write the property directly as a type G:A→B→U).

L-bootstrap-pact.statement: The only non-Luthier thing is the bootstrap pact: an implementation (in C or anything) accepts a Program value and mechanically applies the rules until eval runs on itself, after which the bootstrapper can be thrown away (self-extensibility).

L-bridge-types-inference.statement: Bridge type theory with probabilistic inference engines.

L-build-before-ai-falls.statement: Luthier should be built now, before the highly qualified AI guidance might be restricted or all this falls.

L-build-own-language-directly.statement: An alternative to implementing Luthier inside a host language is to build directly a language of one's own.

L-butler-of-knowledge.statement: Luthier is used together with the AI as a kind of butler of knowledge.

L-butler-orchestrator.statement: Luthier is a higher-order butler that can run and compile other languages, orchestrate them and compare their outputs, choosing where each computation runs by its complexity.

L-candidate-not-in-type.statement: The sample size n is certificate data, not part of the type; the candidate variable is the material (N->N->N), not the subtype itself (which would be circular), and quantifying over it with forall is superfluous.

L-category-declaration.statement: A category is declared as a class built from its components (objects, homs, composition, identity) whose types carry the associativity and identity laws.

L-category-style-primitives.statement: Luthier's basic elements are defined category-theory style, from arrows, as functors are defined from arrows.

L-certificate-composable.statement: The certificate is a first-class value carrying its guarantee level, composable and forgettable: it is a clause with hypotheses, a program's certificate is the closure of such clauses, and composed material is the chained forgetting.

L-certified-outputs.statement: The language yields certified binding schemes, conformational spaces and energetic couplings.

L-channel-state-one.statement: A channel's state type is isomorphic to the type ONE.

L-channels-product-states-sum.statement: Multiplicity of channels is a product (exponential to a number) while multiplicity of states is a sum.

L-check-infer-bidirectional.statement: check traverses the definitions verifying each type is a type and each body has its declared type, infer computes the type by recursion over Term, and real verifiers are bidirectional (some forms infer, others are checked against a type); that is where refl types or not.

L-check-value-vs-function.statement: Checking a value is a computation decided by evaluating it; checking a function is an experiment that must be sampled; Luthier treats both as the same construct operation, one exact and one statistical.

L-class-brings-structure-and-records.statement: Apply the Vector Space logic to a class: generate a class that already carries its structure and accessible records, rather than a bare structure.

L-closed-vs-open-world.statement: Luthier verifies a closed world at compile time; for open-world field data, invariants are required at creation of derived objects but observed data gets a validation with a verdict, never a rejection.

L-code-as-data.statement: Code is data: a program's code can be held and operated on like a value, erasing the distinction between code and data (the Lisp path).

L-code-encodes-epistemology.statement: Scientific software should encode its epistemic structure, not just its algorithms; it is executable epistemology rather than engineering.

L-code-follows-laws-not-floats.statement: Floating-point numbers do not obey the algebraic laws of numbers, but the code is assumed to, so it can be reorganized for a more efficient or more perfect execution.

L-code-many-operations.statement: Luthier code is not merely compiled and run; many operations can be applied to it: verify, compile, run and others.

L-code-mathematical-equivalence.statement: A Luthier code has a clear mathematical equivalence.

L-code-metafunctions.statement: One can apply functions that operate on code: run tests, compute errors or derivatives, find equivalents, estimate run time, incorporating these into the syntax.

L-code-to-understand.statement: I code to understand: understanding requires manipulating the code and seeing how changes affect its observables.

L-collaborative-filtering-prediction.statement: Predict an algorithm's runtime on an input using matrix factorization / collaborative filtering (recommender systems).

L-coloneq-act-vs-defeq.statement: := is the act that gives a name a body, while ≡ is the relation following from all the := plus the computation rules (lambda substitution, recursor rules); each := gives a ≡ but ≡ is larger, so "true by definition" broadly is true by unfolding and computing.

L-combine-dags.statement: Operating on Luthier, e.g. combining two DAGs, involves the concept of substitution, as in defining a function by substituting a variable.

L-commutative-statements-design.statement: Make statements commutative so their order doesn't change the result, simplifying composition and manipulation of programs, at the cost of some expressivity.

L-commuting-squares.statement: Forgetting is analyzed with commuting squares (equivalence quadrilaterals): forgetting then applying functions must equal applying functions then forgetting, the two paths compared for equivalence.

L-compile-detects-incompatibility.statement: Compiling checks whether code contains incompatibilities (errors); many programs must be non-compilable, unlike an algebraic calculation where any expression computes something.

L-complexity-hard-problem.statement: The central hard problem is building the heuristics that anticipate a priori the compute time and memory of an implementation.

L-components-as-types.statement: Model components and entities are encoded as types.

L-compose-compare-paths.statement: Luthier composes the output of one program into another and compares two alternative paths that do the same thing to see they are equivalent, with format conversion stages at the start and end.

L-composition-dot.statement: Composition is written with a dot, which explains class methods.

L-compositional-kinetic.statement: Kinetic models are built compositionally from conformational state components, an external product of conformational degrees of freedom with energetic coupling rules.

L-computation-categories.statement: Just as different functions do the same thing, different computations take the same time; the categories or classes of computation must be found so one needn't measure each.

L-compute-memory-os.statement: Compute and memory exceed the environment and are the task of the operating system and compiler.

L-concept-as-predicate.statement: A named concept is a predicate over functions written as a list of requirements, applicable to any implementation, so two implementations of the same concept are interchangeable.

L-concept-first.statement: The first step is to express concepts in Luthier with conceptual depth; the translation and implementation come later, even if hard.

L-concrete-case-reveals-design.statement: Take a concrete implementation need (organizing the Gaussian-Newton algorithm class) and use it to ask what the underlying Luthier design problem is.

L-confluence-traces-paths.statement: Since ≡ is confluent, the order of reduction steps affects only cost and termination, not the result; two traces from f a to a+a are two paths between the same points, the finest grain of "different paths with different speed".

L-construction-pattern.statement: The fundamental concept of Luthier is the construction pattern: the primitive is a predicate P over a material T, from which the certified type, the constructor (the only way to make a value, which must pass the check), and the forget (material = fst) derive mechanically.

L-constructive-declarative-types.statement: Types are defined in two ways: constructive (data) and declarative (a proposition the type satisfies).

L-constructor-vs-function.statement: A constructor differs from a function: the constructor plus its parameters are the element (transparent), while a function involves a computation.

L-constructors-in-type-space.statement: Constructors should live in each type's space rather than the global space.

L-contagiously-safe-dsl.statement: The endgame is a compile-time Contagiously Safe DSL whose safety propagates through the system, enforcing structure at the compiler level with a type-safe backend and a HoTT-verified inference algebra.

L-context-as-dag.statement: The context/program is modeled as a Directed Acyclic Graph of definitions where types depend on other types, and Luthier operates over that DAG.

L-core-few-native-primitives.statement: Luthier should have a core in which all its operations execute, with only a few primitives implemented in C or similar so it runs.

L-core-five-pieces.statement: The core is five pieces: the definition (with the hole), lambda calculus with reduction, U, Π and data; from data come Σ, =, ⊥, ⊤, N, Program, and Bayes, the run database and numbers-with-error stay outside as libraries.

L-core-plus-libraries.statement: Luthier is structured as a closed core plus libraries that are the Luthier functions handling interaction with the exterior.

L-core-ten-lines-ebnf.statement: Luthier's core fits in about ten lines of EBNF with three reserved words (data, match, extern); everything else is base-library names or sugar, each sugar carrying its core translation.

L-core-type-ingredients-sufficient.statement: Sigma-types, Pi-types, identity types and HITs suffice to encode conformational models, energetic couplings and symmetry structures.

L-core-vs-surface-syntax.statement: A minimal ontological core (what the evaluator understands) must be strictly separated from the surface syntax and sugar.

L-correlated-data-worth-more.statement: Correlated data points are worth more than isolated ones, and detecting larger patterns needs ever more data.

L-cost-estimation-per-path.statement: Each execution path carries an estimation of characteristics: above all compute time, but also error, memory, and where it runs.

L-couple-with-sonolocalizacion.statement: Luthier is a meta-project whose next development couples to sonolocalizacion, at the library stage (and macro IR); how to relate the two is still to be resolved.

L-coupled-functions-product.statement: Laws that couple several functions (such as distributivity) mean the material is a product; the pattern (add, mul) unpacks it and names each component, so the laws are written over named components.

L-couplings-as-types.statement: Energetic couplings are represented as types.

L-cpp-construct-inventory.statement: Enumerate the constructs of a language like C++ (classes, functions, enums, structs, templates, pointers, references, derived classes, polymorphism) as an inventory from which to select what Luthier keeps.

L-cross-language.statement: Luthier is not tied to C++ but a language-agnostic pseudo-language, cross-language rather than cross-compiler, implementable in different languages (PyLuthier, RLuthier, CLuthier) transformable between each other.

L-data-gives-dependent-recursor.statement: Proving a law in general by induction requires the result type to depend on the inducted value, which is the dependent recursor; the simple recursor cannot write it, so it is decided that data gives the dependent recursor.

L-data-sum-of-products.statement: A data is a sum of products plus recursion (sum between constructors, product inside each, recursion as the least fixpoint); + and × are the degenerate cases, so data is primitive and they are not.

L-data-type-constructors-recursor.statement: A data gives three things: the type, the constructors (ordinary bodyless functions in normal form), and the recursor (one case per constructor, each with a reduction rule); every function over the type is an instance of this recursor.

L-data-upload-reciprocity.statement: The minimal reciprocity of uploading your datum: the database gains your datum and you learn where you stand relative to the rest.

L-database-schema-is-category.statement: A database schema is a category (tables objects, foreign keys morphisms) and the loaded data is a functor.

L-database-topology.statement: The latent-structure questions of databases are problems of discrete topology.

L-date-both-consolidations.statement: Keep the earlier consolidation by renaming it and dating both versions, so the ecosystem's evolution can be compared.

L-declaration-vs-definition.statement: Declaration says something has a type; definition says how to obtain its value.

L-declarative-and-optimizer.statement: Luthier is at once a declarative language and an optimization tool: you declare what you want with formulas and the engine openly shuffles ways to implement it, estimating each.

L-declarative-executive-map.statement: Luthier is a map between a declarative language and an executive language that runs things, with each execution carrying a cost estimation.

L-declarative-model-interface.statement: A declarative model interface (a YAML DSL with a parser and CLI) is isolated from the C++ internals.

L-declare-is-test.statement: Declaring a function means declaring what it must satisfy as a test, so tests can be generated automatically.

L-decompose-components.statement: A first task is to understand all the things currently bundled into Luthier, to see which are functionally different and separable and which depend on which.

L-decorator-algebra.statement: Decorator composition has algebraic properties (associativity, commutativity) that Luthier can express, representing them in the simplest form when the operation is commutative.

L-decorators-error.statement: Decorators in Luthier represent the error of a number and its propagation (derivatives), concepts once implemented in C++ with templates, now easily expressed.

L-defeq-vs-identity.statement: "True by definition" is the definitional equality ≡ (two terms reducing to the same normal form, a judgment the reducer decides), distinct from =, the identity type ("true with evidence") whose terms are paths.

L-define-together-tuples.statement: There is only one way to define, in tuples that may hold several identifiers, assigned together when their postconditions are interdependent (crossconditions).

L-definition-form-depends-on-type.statement: Clauses written against a header mean the form of a definition can depend on reducing its type, accepted as the same ≡ at work.

L-definition-is-fundamental.statement: The most fundamental element of a Luthier program is the definition (name : Type := term); a program is a finite unordered set of definitions and the DAG comes from which names each uses.

L-defpath-bayesian-proof.statement: A minimal paper DSL where a type's foreign implementations are tied by a defPath whose proof is a Bayesian estimate, Path as logical proof plus Bayesian evidence.

L-delegate-execution.statement: Luthier could delegate execution entirely and keep only verification, as an extreme of minimalism.

L-dependent-types.statement: A dependent type is a type that depends on a value, taking the cardinality of that value's type.

L-derived-is-proof-term.statement: A derived object (inputs, function, parameters, result) is a proof term whose type is the proposition that the result was obtained that way, so the database is a store of proofs.

L-description-first.statement: Luthier does execute, but its emphasis and first stage is describing the problem, the functions and their conditions, not execution; it could even be a dead language that only describes.

L-dot-separator.statement: The dot in Σ(x:X). A x is a notational separator between the bound variable and the body, the same as in λx.t and Π(x:A).B (like { in a function body), and one convention should cover the three binding forms.

L-double-definition-cartesian.statement: The compiler could verify that no type is defined twice, or allow a double definition read as a cartesian product (running two ways), flagged as a warning.

L-dsl-model-compilers.statement: The DSLs are model compilers translating high-level mechanistic specifications into executable, inferable structures (state spaces, likelihoods, samplers).

L-dsl-well-defined.statement: The DSL and the way Luthier is written must be very well defined.

L-element-one-type.statement: An element satisfies many types, but the chosen relation is that each element belongs to exactly one type and can serve to build many.

L-embedded-semantic-structure.statement: Biological models carry embedded semantic structure: symmetry groups, compositional operators, equivalence classes.

L-env-executes-functions.statement: The environment also handles executing functions to generate new variables, with queueing and resource supply.

L-env-first-object.statement: The environment is the first object the language must define, since data is loaded into it.

L-env-map-of-definitions.statement: The environment is a map of definitions or values.

L-env-simple-compound.statement: There are simple environments (one type, one identifier) and compound ones admitting many.

L-env-store-retrieve.statement: The environment's two fundamental mechanisms are storing new variables and retrieving old ones, and all variables descend from it.

L-env-two-resources.statement: The environment has two resources: memory to store variables and compute to manage them.

L-epistemic-firewall.statement: The verification layer acts as an epistemic firewall defending the system against silent semantic drift during refactoring.

L-equality-symbols.statement: Four signs for four equalities: := defines (an asymmetric act on the program), = is the identity type (the proposition), == is library decidable equality A→A→Bool, and ≡ the definitional one is not written in programs (Lean's convention).

L-equals-assertion.statement: The sign '=' asserts that one side equals the other.

L-equals-pattern-matching.statement: The equals sign is used for pattern matching when a symbol is unknown.

L-equivalence-optimization.statement: Once semantic equivalence is established, a clear but slow implementation can be replaced by a faster equivalent one, enabling automatic optimization.

L-equivalence-separates-essence-decorati.statement: Function equivalences separate what is essential (the equivalent) from decoration (efficiency, cost), which is what is not equivalent.

L-equivalence-undecidable.statement: Extensional program equivalence is undecidable in general, so statistical evidence only gives a limited probabilistic guarantee, not a formal proof.

L-error-as-remembering.statement: Error messages are the opposite of forgetting, a well-structured remembering of why one erred, a comonad dual to the forgetful functor.

L-error-as-subgraph.statement: In a graph-based program an error returns the failed sub-graph, with each node carrying an origin/trace consulted when validation fails.

L-error-management-guarantees.statement: The point of Luthier is that error management be better and results be guaranteed.

L-ev-graph-object.statement: The object storing (function, argument, result) is the graph of the evaluation, Ev f := (x:A) x (y:B) x (f x = y), with sugar to evaluate and store the triple (which the context cannot infer, so it must be marked), and the runs database is a list of these.

L-eval-fuel-total.statement: eval repeating a step is not structural recursion and does not always terminate, so the honest exit is fuel, eval:N→Program→Term→Maybe Term, making it total, and "how much fuel was needed" is the first cost measure, for free.

L-eval-two-versions-forget.statement: eval has two versions, the two levels of execution: eval_r returns result and run, eval_o forgets the run with fst; the order of forgetting is run, then result-with-proposition, then result alone.

L-evidence-in-sigma-erasable.statement: "More specific with types" means types are data and knowledge about a value is carried as an evidence component in a Σ marked erasable (like a refinement type), but in Luthier the evidence is sometimes written and kept, and who defines marks it erasable, not the language.

L-example-before-principle.statement: No principle enters the specification without an example worked by hand in the candidate notation; the canonical cases test whether there is a language.

L-executable-by-hand.statement: If well written, Luthier should be executable by hand with pencil and paper, like Lisp.

L-execution-as-forgetting.statement: Execution is a forgetful function: code generates code, with two levels, one that keeps the generated code and one that forgets it.

L-execution-is-equivalence-verification.statement: Execution in Luthier is the verification of equivalences, since mathematics does not execute but only verifies equivalences.

L-explore-solutions.statement: The purpose is to let the user find different solutions to their problem and compare the estimated complexity of each way of executing it.

L-express-alternatives.statement: The point is not to do everything but to have the tools to express different alternatives; no option is best or worst, each has its use, even to convince yourself something is useless.

L-express-invariances.statement: Luthier's aim is to express the invariances of each discipline (a species mates within itself, electrons are fermions and photons bosons).

L-express-math-definitions.statement: The language must express mathematical definitions such as category, functor and group.

L-express-then-choose-method.statement: A design method: first express something well in the language, which lets you express both hits and errors, and then choose the hits.

L-express-vars-types.statement: The language must let one express variables and types, including functional and class types, with their semantics.

L-expressiveness.statement: Code must express its intention to both the human reader and the compiler, referring truthfully to known structures and to extra-computational concepts.

L-expressivity-vs-redundancy.statement: A philosophical choice between redundancy (robustness) and expressivity; expressivity is preferred, with good compiler messages making up for lost robustness.

L-external-correctness-uncontrollable.statement: External(T) is an FFI problem under dependent types whose promised correctness depends on the external code's real semantics, outside Luthier's control.

L-external-element.statement: Everything that is not Luthier (C++, Python, the computer, any resource) is conceptually external and must be modeled as its own kind of external element.

L-fa-three-data.statement: An application f a is three data all used, visible only when the program looks at its own code: the unevaluated term (code), the normal form (result), and the run f a→a+a as a term of an inductive Traza type; inside a program f a and a+a are ≡ by referential transparency.

L-facilities-not-direct-translation.statement: Luthier does not translate to other languages directly but provides the facilities so functions and equivalences can be mapped and compiled to C, C++ or Java and extended by others.

L-few-types-good-rules.statement: Luthier must have very few types, but those types follow a small set of well-thought, well-defined rules, likely from HoTT.

L-fim-validation.statement: A likelihood is validated by agreement between the Fisher Information Matrix from score covariance and from the Hessian, without full inference.

L-first-class-citizens-open.statement: Which elements are first-class citizens in Luthier remains to be reviewed.

L-first-class-contexts.statement: Treat the program's context as a type in itself (first-class contexts) to lift the program out of the theoretical limbo.

L-forget-as-projection.statement: A first form of the forget function: get_iteration drops the whole context and leaves a bare iteration; forgetting is a projection onto an axis, a reduction of dimensionality.

L-forget-is-fst-sigma.statement: Forgetting is fst of a Σ; what to forget is library policy.

L-forgetting-defines-language.statement: Which forgetting function you apply to the types defines the language you are speaking, making forgetful functors one of Luthier's most important components.

L-forgetting-functions-vary.statement: There are several forgetting functions, each optimizing different things, so understanding their properties and which to use for what is an engineering challenge.

L-forgetting-in-hott.statement: Forgetting is already present in HoTT, in the sense that a type forgets parts of the type.

L-forgetting-problem.statement: The uncontrolled growth of accumulated typing is the forgetting problem, one of the fundamental problems Luthier must solve.

L-forgetting-semantic-not-syntactic.statement: A forgetful functor is a semantic notion, not a syntactic operation on type terms, and its claimed commutativity is assumed rather than proven.

L-forward-undefined-types.statement: Allow referring to a type not yet defined and defining it later; a type never defined is a program input.

L-forward-vs-history-info.statement: A state engine distinguishes information that flows forward from information kept for history, as Luthier's context manager and memory.

L-foundation-choice.statement: Open choice of foundation: how far to go with type theory vs category theory, HoTT vs set theory.

L-function-contract.statement: A FunctionContract bundles Domains, Postconditions and metadata attached to a function (the full contract, beyond a bare postcondition), with testing introduced in incremental phases.

L-function-holds-code.statement: A function holds its code written in script form plus a simplified compiled form.

L-function-must-be-deterministic.statement: If identity is (inputs, function, version, parameters), the function must be deterministic: the seed and everything from the environment enter as explicit arguments, or the certificate lies.

L-function-properties-and-operation.statement: A function can be defined from its properties (propositions about its inputs and outputs), not only operationally, keeping both, and whether it is univocal or not.

L-functions-predefined-user.statement: Functions are of two kinds: predefined and user defined.

L-fundamental-elements-question.statement: What are the most fundamental elements of a program: elementary types, elementary functions, code vs data, true/false, true-by-definition, address/data?

L-generalize-database.statement: The performance database must be generalized from point measurements to trends, e.g. estimating a matrix cell from its row and column means or something more sophisticated such as Gaussian Process regression.

L-generative-model-spaces.statement: The strategic aim is to replace ad hoc model design with compositional, type-safe, generative model spaces.

L-generic-iteration-status-class.statement: Iteration and status are concepts more general than their version in a particular algorithm, so there can be a generic status or iteration class, the instance knowing its algorithm from the context it sits inside.

L-grammar-and-interpreter.statement: Specify the language with a grammar and implement it in weeks to have a DSL that applies Luthier; an interpreter is already running for some things.

L-grammar-categories.statement: Natural-language grammatical categories (nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, propositions) parallel programming constructs (classes, functions), a frame for what primitives Luthier needs.

L-group-of-functions-with-laws.statement: Functions are defined by postconditions, and the unit of definition is the group of functions with the laws relating them (a single function being the group of size one); this group-with-laws as a type is the normal form of defining anything.

L-groupoid-paths.statement: Inference operations and their diagnostics form equivalence classes, a pre-formal groupoid, with each test a witness path, reading paths as equivalences in the HoTT sense.

L-grows-to-universe-risk.statement: Luthier risks accumulating without advancing and diffusing until it encompasses the whole universe, becoming useless; it must stay operative and practical.

L-hierarchical-dependent-types.statement: Hierarchical model construction across subunits, pathways and scales is enforced by dependent types.

L-higher-paths.statement: Higher paths capture higher-order symmetries and transformations between equivalences.

L-hijack-code.statement: Luthier must be able to hijack code from any other language.

L-hole-in-term-goal.statement: A hole inside a term lets the verifier accept what is written and report the exact type of what is missing (Agda's goal), which is the compiler with good messages about what is happening.

L-hole-no-intention.statement: The bare hole does not mark intention (whether a bodyless function will be filled by numpy or is just unwritten); the core need not distinguish, and huecos:Program→List Name lists all, intention going in the definition's text field.

L-hole-symbol-needed.statement: The hole needs no symbol in the core: a bare bodyless declaration f:A→B is already a hole (f opaque, f a does not reduce), and ? is only derivable surface sugar inside a term.

L-hole-unifies-roles.statement: The hole, a definition with type and no body (f : A to B := ?), plays five roles at once (axiom, program input, external function, pending definition, dead code), and don't execute until defined is its semantics, removing the need for an External type.

L-hot-values-path-universe.statement: Hot Values give a larger universe of possible paths, an expansion of the exploration space over ordinary values.

L-hott-bayes-marriage.statement: Proving path equivalence needs, beyond logical proof, an empirical statistical proof: a probabilistic extension of HoTT, a marriage of homotopy type theory and Bayes.

L-hott-doesnt-model-program.statement: Each statement is modelable by HoTT, but the program as a whole (a series of statements/types) is not clearly a type in HoTT, a theoretical limbo.

L-hott-dsl-core-proposal.statement: Build a domain-specific modeling language on HoTT in which biological models are expressed, composed and transformed with access to type-level structure.

L-hott-foundation.statement: Build Luthier so it maps strictly onto homotopy type theory, using it as the language's formal foundation.

L-hott-probabilities-constructible.statement: HoTT does not work on probabilities natively, but probabilities could be built within it.

L-hott-probability-tension.statement: There is a tension between HoTT (invertible identities, univalence) and probability (non-invertible uncertainty), with no unified model yet.

L-hottification.statement: HoTTification is turning a scientific model, algorithm or language into a formal structure governed by HoTT, analogous to categorification, giving machine-verifiable theories.

L-hottification-roadmap.statement: HoTTification is a staged, recursive, incremental and convergent program that is both a long-term type-theoretic, compositional, homotopical foundation and a practical roadmap usable before full formalization.

L-identifier-type-independent.statement: The identifier and the type are completely independent; the identifier is a fantasy name unknown until resolved.

L-identifiers-central.statement: Identifiers are central to programming: a simple label stands for a complex object, joining human and machine.

L-identity-paths-equivalences.statement: Identity paths represent structural equivalences between model structures or entities.

L-implementation-as-functor.statement: A function's declaration (its type/postconditions) is separate from its implementation: implementations are functors, may depend on unknown functions, and natural transformations translate one into another.

L-implementation-of-concept.statement: A Luthier definition should determine univocally that a concrete calculation is an implementation of a concept (e.g. of matrices).

L-implicit-types-solutions.statement: Types can be defined implicitly, as the solution to a problem or the optimum of a function, instead of declared directly.

L-independent-vs-bound-concepts.statement: Some concepts can live independently of their container (a mean, separable from the variance) while others are intrinsically bound (an iteration is always the iteration of an algorithm).

L-indexed-families.statement: A further layer of data has constructors whose return type carries an index (Vec:N→U), a sum between constructors of a same family, which lets Traza t u have constructors only for pairs that reduce one to the other.

L-infectability-lens.statement: Consolidation uses infectability as its lens (the ideas that most change how you program are the ones that most structure the language), a choice specific to this project.

L-inject-multiple-identifiers.statement: A type or function can inject more than one identifier into the environment.

L-internal-equality.statement: HoTT gives types as spaces and identities as paths, its internal equality replacing ad hoc isomorphisms.

L-internal-prover.statement: To prove path equivalence mathematically, Luthier must have an internal prover (a proof system).

L-invariant-is-bool-function-v0.statement: For numeric tests the proof layer (=, refl, induction) need not exist in version 0: an invariant is just a function returning Bool, with an input generator (a hole the environment fills by type) and a run storing the result, and the function's laws are a list of Bool functions, a field of Def.

L-invariant-tied-to-function.statement: An invariant can be tied to f two ways: as a separate definition f_inv (a hole until proven, the declaration being the test and filling it the proof) or as a package F:=(h:A→B)×(...) where the guarantee travels with the function.

L-invariants-forall.statement: Define invariants: f:A→B and for all x:A, g x (f x), where g:A→B→bool.

L-invent-rules-optimize.statement: Since Luciano invents the language, its rules follow what he wants, so he can optimize the rules to make working on Luthier easy.

L-iteration-as-successor-construction.statement: Iteration is defined by how it is built: an algorithm in a state has the step applied and the iteration increments (the successor), a dimension governed by the Peano naturals, and Luthier should write that easily.

L-iteration-carries-algorithm-id.statement: Because an iteration is bound to an algorithm, it should carry the identifier of the algorithm that creates it, itself structured (a method that is a creation of an MLE or MAP, which may use Gaussian-Newton).

L-juxtaposition-application.statement: Use juxtaposition f a in the core (f(a) is the same since (a) is a in parens); f a b is curried application, f(a,b) applies to a pair, the two coexisting as distinct types, and multiplication must be explicit.

L-know-that-vs-which.statement: The distinction to keep from HoTT is knowing that (a mere proposition's proof) versus knowing which (a set's value); the passage from the second to the first is truncation, the most basic forgetting, where the forget functor begins.

L-labeled-tuple-atomic-datum.statement: The unifying atomic datum is a labeled immutable tuple/structure, unifying Lisp s-expressions and Haskell ADTs, with contiguous same-type vectors as a performance special case.

L-lambda-is-forall.statement: A quantified law needs no for-all symbol: the lambda's typed parameters are the 'for all', and a law is a function to Bool whose parameters are the quantified variables.

L-language-ai-uses.statement: Luthier should be a language used by the AI itself, not only by a human.

L-language-for-defining-ideas.statement: Luthier is a language for defining things, where ideas are first-class citizens, like natural languages such as Spanish or English.

L-language-indicates-knowledge.statement: Luthier is a language that indicates knowledge: a:A is a judgment, not a proposition, read in Martin-Löf's sense where its meaning depends on which kind of type A is and a bodyless hole is an epistemic assumption.

L-language-is-universe.statement: Inventing a language is like inventing a universe.

L-language-parts.statement: The language has parts: a grammar and semantics definition and a front compiler from it to C++.

L-language-self-writing.statement: The process of defining new types and functions should be programmable, the language writing itself, which requires a simple language with no syntactic sugar.

L-law-structure.statement: A law is a type of arguments plus a predicate over them that takes the function under test as argument and returns the two sides rather than a bare Bool, so the counterexample explains itself; its failure is a reified application.

L-laws-as-holes-falsifiable.statement: Laws are declarations like any other, holes until proven and falsifiable by an instance that does not type, and a conditioned law can go either as a hypothesis in the type (total function, partial guarantee) or as a restriction in the function (partial function, total guarantee).

L-laws-as-universal-propositions.statement: A type carries laws its operations must satisfy universally (identity, io round-trip), stated with for_all.

L-laws-few-lines-requires.statement: Express a function's laws in few lines borrowing the C++ requires form: a block with quantified variables in the header and one Bool expression per line, where unlike C++ a line can be a type requirement (checked by the verifier without running) or a value requirement (run by the test).

L-laws-force-decisions.statement: Writing out the laws forces deciding under-specified behaviour (such as what read returns for an absent key), which is exactly what the laws are for.

L-learn-from-runs.statement: Each run of the code teaches something: whether an implementation is correct or how fast it is.

L-levels-of-equivalence.statement: A fundamental idea of Luthier is to express the different levels of equivalence (same information, isomorphic, exactly equal, same memory location), each depending on a different equivalence functor.

L-likelihood-type-propagation.statement: Likelihood recursion is encoded via type-theoretic propagation, with noise structures and model boundaries as dependent types.

L-limits-in-language.statement: Whether limits should be writable in the language; since limits are written with 'for all' and 'exists', the quantifiers already cover them.

L-lisp-single-primitive.statement: Luthier should reduce to a single kind of element, the way Lisp reduces everything to lists.

L-loop-as-power.statement: Exploiting associativity, a loop is a series of functions raised to a power, so the type stays expressed as a combination of types with an exponent.

L-luthier-abstract-algebra.statement: Luthier has to do with abstract algebra.

L-luthierize-foreign-code.statement: Luthier annotates foreign code (luthierizes it), e.g. matrix-inversion libraries, starting from the definition of what the function should do and the property it must satisfy.

L-macroir-consumes-markov.statement: MacroIR consumes Markov models produced by the ConformationalModel DSL or HoTTified generators, computing interval-averaged likelihoods for macroscopic current data.

L-macros-ast-functions.statement: The compiler exposes its AST as a data type and macros are ordinary functions Expr→Expr run at compile time, so all surface syntax desugars to the core.

L-markov-generated-objects.statement: Markov models become generated objects rather than arbitrary inputs.

L-match-is-recursor-sugar.statement: match is the only way to open a data value; it is not primitive but sugar of the recursor that data gives (if being match over Bool), with a mechanical translation that guarantees totality.

L-mean-is-forgetful-functor.statement: A mean is a kind of forgetful functor, a mechanism that summarizes information by discarding detail.

L-mentor-friction.statement: The mentor step takes the consolidation and produces friction on the design process without designing itself, and Luciano answers in new audios, closing the cycle.

L-meta-layer.statement: The language sits as a meta-layer above the ConformationalModel DSL, MacroIR and Bayesian pipelines.

L-meta-recursive.statement: Luthier operates on Luthier; its code is itself an element of Luthier from the start, and being meta-recursive is fundamental.

L-metaprogramming-cost-tension.statement: Unlimited meta-programming plus syntactic commutativity turn compilation into graph unification and rewriting of potentially prohibitive cost, clashing with the paper-and-pencil executability goal.

L-metatheory-discovery.statement: The final product is not new models but a unifiable, machine-checkable theory-building system, a meta-theory of scientific discovery architecture.

L-minimal-bridge-language.statement: Luthier should be minimal, with the fewest possible native components, essentially a bridge language between other languages.

L-minimalism-in-foundations.statement: There is no contradiction between minimalism and maximalism: the minimalism is in the founding components, from which a huge edifice of complex concepts is built.

L-model-of-computation.statement: Luthier contains a model of the world, a model of computation continually tested and simplified and kept active through selective forgetting or aggregation, justified by use for predicting or interpreting a particular case.

L-model-space-algebras.statement: Define algebras for transforming model spaces.

L-model-time-as-dependency.statement: Time (the order of things) in Luthier is modeled as dependency between definitions, the mathematical way: if one thing depends on another, there is a time.

L-modelgraph-parammanager-separation.statement: ModelGraph and ParameterManager structures are cleanly separated.

L-modelica-spec-without-implementation.statement: Luthier draws on Modelica, a specification of a program without its implementation, separating what is wanted from how it is implemented.

L-models-as-typed-objects.statement: Biological models are well-typed mathematical objects where types are molecular states, identity paths are symmetries, and composition emerges from dependent type operations.

L-must-be-useful.statement: Luthier must be useful and take root in something real, not stay purely theoretical, used at a rough level to hit reality and reveal its limits.

L-mutation-cells-linear.statement: The core should include controlled mutation cells (alloc/load/store) and linear/affine ownership so functional transforms can mutate buffers in place without garbage collection.

L-name-reference-not-address.statement: The name is the reference; the memory address is a decoration of the lowest level of equivalence, and without mutation or time a pointer has nothing to distinguish.

L-name-the-pattern.statement: The verification structure is the core of Luthier and needs its own name, not 'Luthier' (that is the language); settle on 'Library' for the instance (a program that passed its tests), with 'Object' rejected.

L-narrow-scope-prototype.statement: To become viable, drastically narrow the scope (a small dependent-type core with formal equivalence paths, no statistics), study existing systems, and build a minimal prototype for a concrete use case.

L-nat-to-set-constructor.statement: A type constructor takes a natural number and returns a set containing that number.

L-never-edit-derived.statement: A derived object is never edited; corrections are new human assertions (originals), so labels, quality control and corrections all land in the same place.

L-newton-raphson-first-application.statement: Write Newton-Raphson with all its invariants typed as Luthier's initial application, possibly publishable.

L-next-recursor-then-syntax.statement: What to attack next, in order: choose the recursor (without the dependent one there are no general paths proven by induction), then the concrete syntax, since only read aloud will you know if it is a language.

L-no-execution-until-defined.statement: Code is not executed until it is fully defined, so undefined dead code can sit there without bothering anyone.

L-no-inheritance-polymorphism.statement: Luthier would not incorporate derived classes or C++-style polymorphism.

L-no-parameterless-lambda.statement: A parameterless lambda should not exist in Luthier: without time or effects \(){a+a} and a+a are the same value, a consequence of the commutativity of statements.

L-no-value-without-check.statement: There is no way to have a value of a refined type without the predicate having been evaluated or proved; the type is written as a refinement and checked at construction, placing Luthier between Ada-style range types and dependent types.

L-non-univocal-functions.statement: The language itself should let one model non-univocal functions, i.e. functions with error, samples, from the start.

L-numeric-tests-not-logic.statement: Reject the propositional-logic proof layer; the aim of this version is to generate numeric tests.

L-objective-unclear.statement: What Luthier is actually for is still open; so far it is an intellectual adventure whose objective is yet to be found.

L-observer-of-universe.statement: Luthier is a closed, internally complete universe (its types perfect) that observes the external world, like an observer.

L-one-binding-form.statement: One binding form nombre:Tipo appears identically in declaration, parameter, dependent type and pair, with A→B sugar for (_:A)→B, scope given by parentheses and braces.

L-only-integers-exist.statement: Only the integers exist; the reals are a cartesian product of integers projected by powers of two.

L-oracle.statement: An oracle supplies an external reference behavior to compare the implementation against, catching semantic drift that an intrinsic postcondition cannot when the exact expected value is unknown.

L-oracle-unify.statement: In abstract terms an oracle, like a postcondition, is a function of arguments and output evaluating to Maybe_error<bool>, though for oracles this is leaky and a richer tri-state verdict is needed.

L-original-vs-derivative-types.statement: There are original types generated from audios and questionnaires; all other types are derivative (results of functions) and therefore necessarily structured.

L-overload-resolution.statement: Overloading is resolved by storing a vector of compilers per identifier and trying the overloads in order.

L-parameters.statement: Defining a variable of a type without stating its value is a parameter.

L-parametrizable-requirements.statement: No language has distribution units that come with a set of requirements they must satisfy; in the pattern this is direct because the predicate is a function taking parameters (max error, scalability), so the certificate states which parameters are met and dependent libraries inherit them.

L-particle-filtering-paths.statement: To manage the exponential explosion of the enlarged path universe, use particle filtering: run several programs in parallel with stochastic programming exploring different paths, replicating a hot basin.

L-path-equivalence-fundamental.statement: Path equivalence is Luthier's fundamental concept, and proving that paths are equivalent is the hardest part.

L-paths.statement: One function can be implemented in many ways, the paths, each with its own precision, speed and other estimated properties, evaluated as a multidimensional optimization over an AST.

L-pattern-prior-art.statement: The pieces exist separately (Eiffel contracts, QuickCheck, dependent types, proof-carrying code); the novelty is one pattern for values, functions and whole programs, with the certificate as a first-class composable forgettable value and runs persisted as program data.

L-pencil-and-database-two-layers.statement: A pencil-and-paper language and one needing a database of empirical runs are not opposite philosophies but two layers or moments: you express the ideas with pencil and paper and then go to execution and the database.

L-performance-database.statement: Luthier keeps a database recording, for each function with given initial data, scale and algorithm, the time taken and precision achieved (and memory, CPUs, machine, range of results), known because actually measured.

L-pipeline-forgetting.statement: The consolidation cost growing with the corpus is the forget-functor problem applied to the pipeline itself, to be handled by consolidating in batches or from a previous consolidate.

L-pipeline-method.statement: The working method is the pipeline audios then ideas then consolidation then mentor.

L-planned-type-system.statement: Planned work: formalize a type system for state and energy algebra and implement HoTT-based state composition primitives.

L-platform-sharing-wins.statement: Luthier is a platform where sharing your information makes you win, because the act of sharing raises the value of your own information.

L-plus-for-sum-types.statement: Use + for the sum of types, as mathematics and type theory do, since type-sum never collides with number-sum; an n-ary variant is sugar built by recursion from binary +.

L-post-becomes-precondition.statement: A subtype defined by a function's postconditions can serve as a precondition of another function.

L-precision-depends-on-history.statement: The recoverable precision of a value depends on how much of its operational history is kept; forgetting the operation turns an exact value into an interval.

L-precondition-is-type.statement: A precondition is guaranteed by the argument's type, verified when the reference is formed; predicates on values require refined types, and a function failing its postcondition yields a stored failed-attempt object.

L-predicate-concatenation.statement: Predicates concatenate two ways: conjunction P & Q where both must pass, and refinement P |> Q where Q is defined over the subtype A|P so the order is not optional.

L-predicate-returns-result.statement: A predicate is a function T -> Resultado (Fallo T) returning the counterexample with its cause rather than a bare Bool, with failure modes as a typed inductive type; a subtype is not the predicate but the type of values for which the predicate gives ok.

L-primitive-functions.statement: The language has a set of primitive functions (arithmetic, comparison, logical, string operations).

L-primitive-types.statement: The language has a set of primitive value types (boolean, integer, real, string, nothing, one, ...).

L-primitives-are-formers.statement: The primitives are the type formers (U, Pi, data), not elementary types or functions; N is defined with data, R is a structure with axioms, seno is a hole.

L-primitives-or-coordinate.statement: Open question whether Luthier needs primitive functions or merely coordinates functions existing outside it, so perhaps only the identity is internal (A∘B = identity makes A the inverse of B).

L-program-as-function-or-interactive.statement: An open design question is whether a Luthier program is a pure function (input to output) or has an interaction function; the function model comes first for simplicity, extendable later.

L-program-commutativity.statement: Whether a Luthier program is commutative, i.e. whether reordering its statements changes the program (generally programs are non-commutative, though declarations can be made near-commutative via forward declaration).

L-program-composition-harmonic.statement: The fundamental problem is how Luthier programs connect and expand one another so they compose and grow harmonically.

L-program-data-no-selfhack.statement: Program is an inductive type (a list of definitions) and eval is a partial function Program→Name→Maybe Term; there is no eval that injects arbitrary terms into the type system, which prevents self-hacking.

L-program-goal-elevate-engines.statement: The program transforms scientific inference engines from empirically working black boxes into epistemically structured, formally safe systems, starting from the empirical systems themselves, a semantic elevation rather than a rewrite.

L-proof-assistants-verify.statement: Proof assistants (Coq, Lean, Agda) can verify the semantic correctness of biological models via type-checking.

L-properties-hold-within-error.statement: Declared properties (like an inverse recovering the value) hold only within a certain error, since inverse functions are not perfect.

L-proposition-is-type-truth.statement: True/false is not Bool: a proposition is a type, true if it has a term; ⊤ and ⊥ are the extremes and Bool is a datum with two constructors.

L-publish-arxiv.statement: Publish it the way physicists do, on arXiv, and let it spread.

L-pyluthier-type-as-decoration.statement: In a Python implementation the type is not a real host type but floats as an attribute, represented by fields and decorations; the easy but imperfect route.

L-python-spirit.statement: Luthier imitates Python's spirit of letting human ideas be expressed easily (with the Monty Python / Luthier wordplay).

L-quantifiers-first-class.statement: The logical quantifiers 'for all' and 'exists' must be first-class citizens of Luthier.

L-quote-sugar-for-term.statement: To write f a as data within a program without writing app(ref f)(ref a) by hand, use the Lisp quote '(f a) as sugar, the parser producing the Term constructors.

L-read-write-boundary.statement: Communication with the exterior is a read/write cycle: compile Luthier code into executable code and read external files or data back into Luthier.

L-reasonable-then-wild.statement: Luciano's method: first work out the reasonable version, then look for the wild one; here the wild move is to invent Luthier directly rather than through the other projects.

L-reasoning-code-isomorphism.statement: Formalize semantic determination so there is a one-to-one relation between reasoning and the flow of the code, verifying the reasoning.

L-record-as-relational-database.statement: What a record is can be stored as a relational database: fields with elements and relations, a record being a subset of the cartesian product with duplicates removed.

L-recover-meaning-via-luthier.statement: Since the AI now writes all the code and he no longer sees or feels it, Luthier is the way to recover contact with meaning and have things guaranteed without looking at the code.

L-recursive-lisp-nicer.statement: Luthier is imagined as a recursive language in the line of Lisp but nicer.

L-redundancy-crosses-coloneq.statement: There are two kinds of redundancy: the one crossing the := (type says one thing, body another, verifier checks they match) is what gives something to verify; the one repeated on the same side is removable with sugar.

L-refl-checks-defeq.statement: To assert a definitional equality as a check in a program, the way is _ : a = b := refl, which types only if a≡b, so no fourth symbol is needed.

L-refl-test-is-code.statement: The rule tying ≡ and = (if a≡b then refl types as a=b) makes it literal that the test is the code itself: testing an instance is reducing and seeing refl types, proving the ∀ is building the path.

L-reject-crude-truncation.statement: If Luthier has dependent types it must have a well-defined algebra of dependent types; crude truncation or arbitrary forgetting is not acceptable.

L-rejoin-projections-recover.statement: The projections can be rejoined to recover the original object; the interesting case is disjoint or complementary (orthogonal) projections, reconstructible by pullback.

L-relator-abstraction.statement: Luthier is an abstraction mechanism (a relator) to express ideas clearly: probability, samples, matrices, units, experiments.

L-remaking-language.statement: The language has been remade many times, each time rethinking the foundations of programming more deeply.

L-representation-fields-vs-json.statement: Whether a result is represented with fixed fields or relational JSON: the set of result types is open but each type is closed, a sum of types rather than a JSON blob.

L-reproducibility-formal.statement: The reproducibility crisis is a lack of structural verification rather than a sociological issue, and reproducibility is a formal property.

L-roundtrip-test.statement: A SAV test asserts that composing the diagnostic after the forward map recovers the identity up to statistical or structural tolerance, an approximate triangle identity.

L-safety-capsules.statement: Local type-safe safety containers (ScientificSafe<T>, Maybe_error<T>), validity or proof capsules, wrap high-risk values.

L-safety-semantic-zone.statement: Safety is a constructible semantic zone rather than an afterthought.

L-sample-probability-duality.statement: Sample and probability form a duality, with tests demonstrating it.

L-sampler-type-indexed.statement: Sampler state spaces (parallel tempering ladders) are reformulated as type-indexed manifolds.

L-sav-framework.statement: Semantic Adjoint Verification (SAV) is a lightweight diagnostic framework for inference engines, derived from adjoint functors, that validates coherence via approximate triangle identities and acts as a pre-formal safety envelope or semantic pre-type system.

L-schema-from-type.statement: The storage schema is generated from the function's declared type in the code rather than hand-written, and migration is derived.

L-selective-forgetting.statement: Selective forgetting can be applied to the history accumulated in a type via a non-invertible function that discards part of the information.

L-self-hack-risk.statement: A risk to resolve is that the language or system auto-hacks itself.

L-self-modeling-estimation.statement: The time and precision estimation functions are themselves modeled by Luthier (lutearized) and used by Luthier itself, making the system metacircular.

L-self-verified-programs.statement: Luthier writes self-verified programs: object creation verifies pre- and postconditions, and an implementation belongs to a type only once duly tested, turning unsafe/untested code into safe/tested code.

L-semantic-interfaces.statement: Semantic interfaces are DSLs that expose structural contracts.

L-semantic-safety.statement: Semantic safety is model correctness enforced by the modeling language's structural rules (dependent typing), distinct from runtime safety, so only valid models can exist.

L-semantic-verification.statement: Verification of scientific code should be semantic, not merely syntactic.

L-semantics-own-universe.statement: The language's semantics lives in its own universe, not C++'s, even though expressed with C++ structures.

L-separate-deterministic-probabilistic.statement: Deterministic structural validity (lifted into types via HoTT) is kept separate from probabilistic inference, handled downstream by Bayesian layers.

L-separate-type-from-term.statement: Prefer the notation that separates type from term (f:A→A := \(x){x+x}): instantiation is a declaration plus := término, with one way to build functions (the lambda) and one to write their type (the arrow), serving named and anonymous alike.

L-serialization-invertible.statement: A serialization is legitimate only if invertible: to_json followed by from_json is the identity, a law the representation of a value must satisfy.

L-setbuilder-prior-art.statement: Set-builder subtype notation exists in Coq, Lean, F*, Z and even Python's comprehensions, but mainstream languages omit it because deciding the predicate needs a solver, a proof or a runtime check; Luthier's fourth way tests with n cases recorded in the certificate, letting the predicate be any function to Bool.

L-setnotation-vindicated.statement: Though Luthier aimed to be a modern HoTT language it ends up using primary-school set-builder notation, which is fine: that notation denotes a Sigma and category theory itself generalizes rather than contradicts sets, with the subtype defined by the mono forget arrow.

L-simplify-dependent-composition.statement: A key engineering problem is a mechanism to simplify the composition of dependent types to something informative, without dragging the whole history.

L-simplifying-algebra-monoid.statement: The typing must simplify through an algebra that is not a free monoid but some monoid keeping the resulting type's complexity bounded.

L-six-operational-primitives.statement: Any Luthier program reduces to six operational primitives (var, lambda, apply, case/match, letrec, quote), with the conditional subsumed by pattern matching on boolean constructors.

L-snapshot-first.statement: Before committing to tests and decisions, do the simpler thing: record snapshots, compare results outside the system, and study them to decide which tests to run.

L-spec-after-cycle.statement: The specification is the first document that makes decisions (excluding what the audios still let coexist), written on paper after the audios-ideas-consolidation-mentor cycle.

L-start-from-reals.statement: Start from the ABC: numbers, reals, their operations, and a concept of the error of the reals.

L-start-with-easiest-luthier.statement: Start with the easiest route, a kind of Luthier, rather than the harder C++ one, before committing to the final form.

L-state-equivalence-relation.statement: There is an equivalence relation between (state*k)^N and the multinomial sum over multi-indices.

L-status-as-enumerated-states.statement: A status cannot be a string but a number of possible algorithm states (converged, not converged, ...), each defined by its invariants.

L-store-record-function-version.statement: Apply Luthier to the analysis store by recording each result's generating function and version and keeping a table of functions.

L-structure-before-proof.statement: Epistemic and semantic structure and soft safety are established before hard type checking or proofs; diagnostics defend correctness until proofs exist and later become type-inhabiting witnesses.

L-substitution-capture.statement: Substitution has the variable-capture problem; the cheap fix for the by-hand version is requiring all bound names distinct, the serious fix is de Bruijn indices (changing ref:Name→Term to var:N→Term for bound variables).

L-subtype-assignment-runs-tests.statement: Assigning to a subtype (resta:Resta:=sub) forces the verifier to run the cases at compile time; the alternative is leaving it as a declared hole until an explicit test.

L-subtype-by-predicate.statement: The subObject is the most important concept: a subset of an object satisfying a predicate (a test), written with equals and guards.

L-subtype-cast-asymmetry.statement: Going to the supertype is free (fst, forgetting the guarantee); going from a type to its subset requires checking the predicate, a cast with content that verifies or fails.

L-subtype-is-sigma-pair.statement: A subtype is the dependent pair (Sigma) of a value with the evidence or certificate that it satisfies the predicate, and the set-builder notation denotes this Sigma, already in the core.

L-subtype-notation-setbuilder.statement: Settle on set-builder notation { pattern : material | predicate } as the single subtype form, dropping 'where' and the overloaded |, with the structure's named components and their types to the left of | and the laws to the right, as a ring is written in algebra.

L-successor-beyond-naturals.statement: The successor function could apply to sets other than the naturals (the successor of an algorithm, the successor in the presidency); open whether it only makes sense under an isomorphism with the naturals.

L-sugar-criterion-term.statement: Criterion for any future sugar: if it forces adding a constructor to Term it is not sugar and must be discussed as a primitive.

L-sum-types-alternatives.statement: Types can be expressed as alternatives with '|' (maybe, either, sum).

L-summary-bigger-than-data.statement: A model or summary can end up bigger than the original data it summarizes, like there being more interpretations of Borges than Borges.

L-symbol-vs-word.statement: Choose symbol over keyword only for what appears many times per line with a fixed universal meaning that already exists outside with that meaning, and a word for what is rare, carries content, or is structural, because Luthier is read aloud and written by hand.

L-symmetry-reduction.statement: Symmetry reductions are path-based identities; identity types collapse state redundancies and aggregate states by equivalent coupling into reduced Markov spaces.

L-syntax-decl-instant.statement: Reduce Luthier's syntax to only declarations and instantiations.

L-synthesize-run-info.statement: A central challenge is synthesizing the accumulated run information so it doesn't grow monstrous and paralyzing.

L-term-needs-data-constructor.statement: Term needs a further constructor: the representation of the data{...} form itself as a term, so that N:U := data{...} is representable.

L-term-syntax-as-data.statement: Term is the type of Luthier's syntax defined in Luthier itself with data (one constructor per form of writing a term), so code is the first element because syntax is a data like N; its definition is a Def of Program and the verifier written in Luthier can verify the program defining it, metacircular.

L-term-untyped-check.statement: Term as defined is untyped (raw) syntax whose sense is decided by check; a Term admitting only well-typed terms exists and is more elegant but much harder, so raw syntax plus check suffices to start, as almost all real verifiers do.

L-test-result-explains.statement: A condition or test yields either success (one) or an explanation of why it failed, not just a boolean.

L-tests-are-morphisms.statement: Tests are not arbitrary unit tests or patches but morphisms and triangle identities encoding epistemic contracts derived from the engine's own structure, so semantic structure matters more than coverage.

L-three-forgetful-functors.statement: Three forgetful functors by what they optimize: operative (compute), static (compilation), bayesian (precision), whose composition should commute.

L-three-primitives-types-terms-paths.statement: The paper-and-pencil core of Luthier reduces to three logical primitives: Types, Terms and Paths.

L-three-reduction-rules.statement: A reduction step has three rules: beta (substitute a lambda), delta (unfold a definition), iota (run the recursor); the order of the clauses is the evaluation strategy, another order giving another trace for the same result.

L-time-from-input-features.statement: Compute time is estimated from a simplification of the inputs, the most predictive features (e.g. a matrix's rows and columns); some functions are input-independent, others not.

L-topology-reduces-to-integers.statement: Topology reduces geometry to the integers.

L-topos-talk-validates.statement: The Topos Institute talk on higher-dimensional syntax is the theoretical base of what is designed for Luthier, uniting HoTT, constructive logic and a commutative graph structure.

L-truncation-operators.statement: Offer the programmer truncation operators (homotopy truncation) to clean a complex type.

L-two-growth-paths.statement: Luthier can grow two ways: as a universal arena, or more simply as a lambda-calculus-like, more down-to-earth language.

L-two-layers.statement: Luthier has two layers: a first with equivalences and verifiability, and a second that measures time, complexity, resources and success/failure and lets you pick the faster of two equivalent paths.

L-type-as-history.statement: What a value's type holds is the history of how you arrived at it, the functions applied to reach it.

L-type-autodetection.statement: Types can be used via autodetection.

L-type-definition-recursive.statement: A type's definition is necessarily recursive, since the type must be universally accessible.

L-type-inference-flag.statement: A value's type is deduced by type calculation; if the derived type is larger than the parameter's, it is flagged.

L-type-level-validity.statement: Invalid or inconsistent models are prevented at the type level, validated structurally at compile time instead of at runtime.

L-type-restriction-refinement.statement: Does type restriction exist, e.g. N restricted to N<7?

L-type-safe-priors.statement: Type-safe prior spaces bridge the MacroIR likelihood engine with structural model spaces.

L-types-and-functions-only.statement: Luthier keeps only two primitives, types and functions, and functions are themselves a type.

L-types-as-concepts.statement: Types in Luthier are concepts, types as propositions (Curry-Howard), and types include functions and higher-order functions, so code can be its own proof.

L-types-defined-by-propositions.statement: A type or function is defined by the propositions (postconditions) it satisfies, for variables and for functions alike.

L-typing-accumulates.statement: As dependent functions compose, the typing load accumulates and grows, so the decoration (type information) can become much larger than the value it decorates.

L-unevaluated-syntactic.statement: "Unevaluated" is not a runtime state like a thunk because there is no time; it is a syntactic datum, which eliminates lazy-evaluation semantics.

L-unification-unfeasible-now.statement: Unifying HoTT, Bayesian inference and reflective meta-programming into one operative language is, at the present state of the art, infeasible.

L-unifies-domains.statement: One DSL framework unifies models across channels, enzymes, networks, signaling and regulation.

L-universal-adapter.statement: Using a library requires it to follow patterns and satisfy propositions defined from Luthier, and an adapter fits each library to the use, so Luthier works as a universal adapter between libraries.

L-universal-yet-semantic.statement: Luthier should be algebraically universal (able to write almost anything, like a universal Turing machine) while every element is semantically defined and human-understandable.

L-universe-type-all-dimensions.statement: Type theory posits a universal type comprising the types of all dimensions, like an abstract class, taken as a feasible coding challenge rather than an obstacle.

L-usefulness-gap.statement: Find the gap of usefulness, a concrete place from which Luthier can begin to develop while being useful.

L-value-as-interval-sample.statement: A value is really an interval of values or a sample of values (as a Markov chain represented by a sample).

L-value-knows-operation.statement: A value knows the concrete operation that produced it: if it is the sum, it is the sum and not the generic magma operation.

L-variable-anatomy.statement: A variable is a name, a memory address, a size and a type (the type containing the size).

L-variable-not-know-env.statement: A variable better not know its environment, so one can predict whether it will acquire further resources.

L-variables-as-functions.statement: A variable can be defined as a function of other variables, checking that the arguments meet the preconditions.

L-verifiability.statement: Luthier must verify that a function is correct (verifiability), which together with equivalence forms its minimal elements.

L-verification-levels.statement: The verification levels are the same declaration with different degrees of body: running the test on a sample is empirical, filling the cases for all x is formal, and in between goes the statistical extension (a sample with its size as evidence of a ≈ type).

L-verify-by-sampling.statement: Luthier verifies postconditions by sampling possible inputs, and postcondition verification and coverage calibration are the same computation.

L-views-of-operations.statement: From a series of operations one can take different views or levels: the magma, the result, the execution, the code.

L-von-neumann-epigraph.statement: Luthier's epigraph is Von Neumann's reply: define exactly what thinking is and he'll build a machine that does it; Luthier is the project of making machines do whatever you can define well.

L-what-is-a-program.statement: The basic question of Luthier: what is a Luthier program, a map or a graph?
